# The Lighthouse Keeper

Samuel had kept the Beacon Point lighthouse for thirty-seven years, watching over the rocky Maine coast with the dedication of a man who understood that his solitude served a purpose. The white tower rose 120 feet from the grey stone, its light cutting through fog and darkness every single night without exception.

He climbed the spiral stairs each evening with the same careful rhythm, his weathered hands trailing along the iron railing. The light room at the top had become his cathedral—a place of profound stillness where he could watch the Atlantic unfold beneath him. Modern navigation systems had rendered lighthouses mostly ceremonial, but Samuel refused to view his work that way. Some ships still relied on the beacon. Some pilots still looked for it. That was enough.

The isolation suited him. After his wife Eleanor had died, the lighthouse had become not a burden but a gift. The work kept him present, kept him moving through the days with intention. Each night he polished the Fresnel lens until it gleamed like captured starlight. During the day, he maintained the grounds, painted the gallery railing, and kept the logbook with meticulous entries.

He had few visitors. The supply boat came monthly, and occasionally a curious tourist climbed to the top, breathless and amazed, before descending to return to their lives. Samuel never minded these interruptions. He remembered being young, before grief had taught him the value of quiet.

One November morning, a young girl appeared at his door with her grandmother. She was perhaps seven, with curious eyes and a worn backpack. While her grandmother browsed the gift shop in the visitor center, the girl asked if she could stay with Samuel.

"I like it here," she said simply. "It's calm."

Samuel showed her everything. He let her help oil the light mechanism, taught her the proper way to polish brass, explained how the beacon had guided ships to safety for over a century. She listened with the kind of attention children offer when something truly captivates them.

As they descended the stairs, she asked why he stayed.

"Someone has to," Samuel said. "And I like being needed."

She nodded as though this made perfect sense.

After they left, Samuel found himself thinking about succession—about who would keep the light when he could no longer climb those stairs. The question had haunted him increasingly, as if the lighthouse itself worried about abandonment. But that day, watching the girl skip back toward the visitor center, he felt something shift. She would remember this place. Perhaps she would return. Perhaps she would tell others about the keeper who lived in the tower, who kept a solitary vigil so that strangers at sea could find their way home.

That night, Samuel climbed to the light room as always. He polished the lens, switched on the beacon, and watched it sweep across the dark water. The light had always seemed lonely to him, emanating into an indifferent ocean. But perhaps it wasn't lonely at all. Perhaps it was simply faithful—doing its small work in the darkness, trusting that somewhere, someone would see it and be guided safely forward.

Samuel stood there until the first light came, at peace with his choice to stay.
